st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The study accepts that aggregate benchmark performance cannot establish broad legal competence and materially extends the synthesis by showing a second concealment mechanism: high LLM-judge agreement can mask failure to preserve legitimate minority interpretations. Its Thai essay results also reinforce task- and jurisdiction-specific variation, with models overlapping rather than clearly surpassing students.
qs: Claude 4.6 Opus and Gemini 3.1 Pro tie at 20/30, one point below the top human (21); five of the eight LLMs sit at or below the human median (11.5); none clears 21.

The high LLM-panel α reflects systematic convergence on the majority                                                   reading rather than balanced reproduction of both readings; a benchmark that selects its LLM judge                                                   by maximising agreement with a human reference panel will inherit this asymmetry by construction.

st.t: Legal quality: Scoring methods encode different harms
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s premise that legal-quality scores encode distinct judgments and materially develops it by showing that correctness and reasoning quality can produce overlapping or inverted numerical outcomes. It also demonstrates that score interpretation depends on examiner calibration supplied through training and experience, not formal rubric categories alone.
qs: Second, the regulation overlaps and inverts: a correct final answer with unusable reasoning (T4: 0–1) scores strictly below an incorrect final answer with good reasoning (T3: 2–4), so the rubric is not a clean correctness split.
The stability ceiling we measure in Section 6 is on this shared-experience-plus-regulation calibration, not on the rubric axes in isolation.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s task- and context-specific account of legal AI and materially extends it by separating examinee capability from grader suitability. Its results show stronger performance on mechanical doctrinal pattern-matching, difficulty with a more nuanced distinction, and grading convergence that can conceal legitimate interpretive disagreement when the rubric is silent. This strengthens the case for use-specific evaluation rather than inferring general legal competence from a single benchmark or role.
qs: Q2 and Q3 reward more mechanical doctrinal pattern-matching once the candidate has reached the correct final answer, and the LLM mean matches or exceeds the human cohort mean on both.

kp.k: Blinded examination separates legal answering from automated grading
kp.d: The June 2026 preprint reports an early-2026 mock examination involving 42 Thai law students and practitioners preparing for the bar and eight LLMs answering three Civil and Commercial Code essay questions, producing 150 answers. Examiners were unaware that models were included. Phase 2 compared three Bar Council-trained examiners and 26 LLM judges on 15 cross-graded answers, supplying identical questions, grading regulations, gold answers and candidate answers. The study concerns legal evaluation methodology rather than demonstrated changes in legal employment or service delivery.
qs: The three examiners were not informed that any participant was an LLM; the blinding was full, not partial.

Human cross-graders and LLM judges thus received the same four inputs and had no access to the primary grader’s score, to each other’s scores, to per-judge aggregates, or to the participant’s identity.

kp.k: LLM essay performance overlaps the human candidate distribution
kp.d: The reported LLM mean was 13.12/30 versus 12.04 for the 42-person human cohort; total-score standard deviations were 5.28 and 4.65 respectively. Claude 4.6 Opus and Gemini 3.1 Pro scored 20, below the highest human score of 21, while GPT-5.4 Pro scored 16. Models performed worse on average on partnership liability and better on the other two questions. The narrative reports two of eight models passing at 15/30, although Table 2 lists three scores meeting that threshold; these are inconsistent source statements.
qs: The LLM distribution overlaps the human distribution rather than dominating it.
Two of eight LLM examinees clear that threshold (25%), against 15 of 42 students (35.7%).

kp.k: Grading disagreement concentrates at an ambiguous rubric boundary
kp.d: The authors distinguish final-answer correctness against a gold answer from interpretive assessment of reasoning quality. On three contested Q2 answers omitting the decisive Section 1023/1 citation, examiner A awarded 1–2 while B and C awarded 6–8. They interpret these as coherent competing applications of a regulation that does not resolve whether the omission makes reasoning unusable or merely incomplete. Human and anchor-LLM agreement was identical at α = 0.75 on pooled Q1/Q3 answers; the five-answer Q2 slice produced α = −0.34 for humans and 0.68 for anchor LLMs.
qs: The regulation does not adjudicate between the two parsings.
The whole-panel gap is a property of three specific items at the regulation-silent boundary, not of base-rate disagreement on bar-essay scoring.

kp.k: Higher LLM agreement does not establish superior legal validity
kp.d: Across 15 answers, the three-model anchor panel—Claude 4.6 Opus, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.4 Pro—reportedly achieved Krippendorff α = 0.77 versus 0.36 for humans. Within-cell standard deviations were 0.71 and 1.32 respectively. The authors caution that agreement measures convergence, not coverage of legitimate interpretations or an independently established correct grading standard. Removing the three contested answers narrowed the comparison to human α = 0.73 and LLM α = 0.79.
qs: The high LLM-panel α reflects systematic convergence on the majority reading rather than balanced reproduction of both readings;
the validity anchor co-depends on which examiner is nominated as ground truth.

kp.k: Models predominantly approach the majority human grading interpretation
kp.d: Using contested-answer means, the study classified 22 of 26 models as B/C-direction, three as intermediate and GPT-5.4 Nano alone as A-direction. The thresholds were at least 5.0 for B/C-direction and at most 3.0 for A-direction, so direction did not require reproducing the human score band. Nano's mean was 2.33 and its full-vector correlation with A was 0.223; it did not consistently reproduce A's 1–2 band. The authors report majority-direction convergence across the tested model sizes, vendors and price tiers, while acknowledging sensitivity of precise counts to classification thresholds.
qs: No LLM in the 26-judge panel reproduces A’s reading of the regulation-silent boundary.

A judge is in A-direction if its contested mean is at most 3.0 (within 1 unit of A’s band); in B/C-direction if its contested mean is at least 5.0 (within 1 unit of B/C’s band); in the middle otherwise.

kp.k: Human-average evaluator selection can suppress minority interpretations
kp.d: The authors argue that selecting an LLM judge to maximise agreement with a human aggregate favours the majority interpretation when two of three reference examiners share it. This is a methodological implication of the reported reference-panel composition, not evidence that the majority reading is legally better. They recommend identifying interpretive cases before selecting judges and evaluating coverage of multiple legitimate human readings rather than treating their average as a single authoritative target.
qs: A benchmark that selects an LLM judge by maximising agreement with a human reference panel will inherit the B/C parsing by construction;
Evaluate LLM judges against multiple legitimate human readings on interpretive cases instead of a single averaged target; report which readings the LLM panel covers and which it misses.

kp.k: Legal examinee skill does not credential evaluator selection
kp.d: Among eight models used in both roles, seven took B/C-direction and Qwen 3.5 Plus occupied the intermediate category. The lowest-scoring examinee, Grok 4.1 Fast at 8/30, had the strongest relative B/C alignment by the authors' correlation-difference metric. The association between examination total and this metric was −0.34 across eight models and −0.90 after excluding Qwen. The authors explicitly describe this inverse association as post-hoc, statistically insignificant at n = 8 and dependent on outlier exclusion; their explanation involving recognition versus construction of legal reasoning remains speculative.
qs: The clean version of the role-separation claim uses the eight examinees as evidence that examinee skill does not credential judge selection.
We flag this finding as exploratory and report it for completeness; it is not statistically significant at n = 8, it depends on outlier exclusion, and it is post-hoc.

kp.k: Automated graders exhibit distinct scoring failure modes
kp.d: The authors diagnose Claude Haiku 4.5 as compressing the 15-answer scale into only 3.5 and 7.5; GPT-5.4 Mini as rewarding correct conclusions despite faulty reasoning; and GPT-5.4 Nano as penalising reasoning omissions severely but inconsistently. Mini's contested mean of 7.83 placed it in B/C-direction despite correlation of −0.21 with examiner B, illustrating that similar average generosity is not equivalent to agreement on individual answers. These are model-specific observations under the tested prompting configuration.
qs: Every one of its 15 cross-graded scores is either 3.5 or 7.5 (Table 7).
Mini collapses onto the deterministic axis: final answer correct ⇒ upper band, regardless of reasoning quality.
Haiku coarsens the scale to a two-value bucket, so neither axis can drive a mid-range score.

kp.k: Repeatability and reference inputs materially affect grading stability
kp.d: Three additional seeds at temperature 0 produced 135 anchor-panel judgments. Reported within-judge cross-seed α values were 0.998 for Claude, 0.945 for Gemini and 0.877 for GPT-5.4 Pro; anchor-panel α across seed slices ranged from 0.76 to 0.82. Withholding the regulation reduced panel α from 0.77 to 0.57, and withholding the gold answer reduced it to 0.47, while humans retained both inputs. These tests support repeatability within the configuration, not legal correctness or equivalence to human working conditions in the ablations.
qs: Within-judge cross-seed Krippendorff α is 0.998 for Claude, 0.945 for Gemini, and 0.877 for GPT-5.4 Pro.
Humans retain both inputs throughout in all configurations.
The panel direction (LLM α > human α) survives both.

kp.k: Small samples limit professional and cross-jurisdictional conclusions
kp.d: The authors limit the evidence to three Thai partnership and corporate-law questions, one rubric, three human examiners and 15 cross-graded answers. Examiners were deliberately not pre-calibrated. They acknowledge public-law doctrinal contamination, configuration dependence, wide confidence intervals and uncertainty about transfer to other jurisdictions or expert domains. Targeted fine-tuning, retrieval and minority-reading exemplars are proposed research directions, not demonstrated remedies. They expressly reject using the findings for individual certification decisions.
qs: Whether other legal regulations have analogous regulation-silent zones, and whether other free-form expert-graded NLP tasks (medical case reasoning, scientific writing review, code-review essays) exhibit similar asymmetric LLM convergence, is an open empirical question.
We do not test whether targeted fine-tuning on minority-reading examples alleviates the asymmetric convergence;
Any findings and analyses are intended for research on legal-reasoning evaluation methodology and should not be used for individual assessment or certification decisions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors claim that automated legal-essay evaluators can exhibit stronger agreement than expert examiners while failing to represent a legitimate minority interpretation of the grading rubric.
pts.d: Akarajaradwong and co-authors report that their three-model anchor panel attained Krippendorff’s α = 0.77 against the three-human panel’s 0.36. They attribute the difference to a specific rubric ambiguity: how severely to penalise a correct conclusion that omits a decisive statutory citation. In the extended panel, 22 of 26 LLMs scored in or toward the majority examiners’ direction, three occupied an intermediate range, and one approached—but did not consistently reproduce—the strict minority reading. The claim concerns agreement in legal-work evaluation, not superior substantive legal correctness or demonstrated replacement of lawyers. The authors explicitly distinguish the anchor models’ intermediate partial-credit reading from exact reproduction of the majority’s grades.

pts.k: Selecting AI evaluators for agreement with an aggregated expert reference can embed the majority’s interpretation and exclude minority readings.
pts.d: The authors argue that a benchmark optimising agreement with a two-to-one human majority will favour evaluators aligned with that majority. This is a methodological implication drawn from the observed scoring pattern, rather than a separately tested deployment intervention. They recommend auditing interpretive ambiguities and evaluating coverage of multiple legitimate readings instead of relying on a single average target or agreement statistic. They further argue that model scale alone does not resolve the observed asymmetry; targeted training or alternative selection methods remain untested possibilities.

pts.k: The authors report student-range performance on Thai legal essays and argue that essay-writing capability does not credential a model as an evaluator.
pts.d: In Phase 1, eight LLMs averaged 13.12/30 versus 12.04/30 for 42 human participants, with substantial overlap and model totals ranging from 8 to 20. In Phase 2, the same eight models did not reproduce the minority examiner’s direction, and the lowest-scoring examinee had the strongest relative majority-cluster alignment. The authors characterise the inverse relationship between exam score and relative cluster alignment as exploratory, post-hoc and not statistically significant at n = 8. Their implication is role-specific evaluation: generating legal reasoning and grading an answer with a supplied rubric and reference answer are different tasks. Relative majority alignment is not itself established as grading accuracy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a two-phase mock-examination experiment, shared-input cross-grading, qualitative grading comments and robustness checks.
pts.d: The working paper reports 150 essays from 42 human participants and eight LLMs answering three Thai Civil and Commercial Code questions. Examiners were blinded to the inclusion of AI answers. Five participants’ answers across three questions supplied 15 cross-graded cells for three Bar Council-trained examiners and 26 LLM evaluators. Each evaluator received the question, official regulation, reference answer and candidate answer. Detailed analyses identify three contested Q2 cells as driving the central disagreement. On the ten Q1/Q3 cells, the human and anchor-model panels each reportedly achieved α = 0.75; excluding the three contested cells yielded 0.73 and 0.79 respectively. The anchor panel underwent 135 additional seed-probe judgements, 5,000 bootstrap resamples and input ablations. Withholding the regulation reduced anchor agreement to 0.57; withholding the reference answer reduced it to 0.47. Translated examiner comments and model explanations support the authors’ interpretation that the central disagreement concerns the treatment of an omitted citation. These are reported research findings, not evidence of operational productivity, market displacement or certification validity.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings are a 2026 research snapshot under a narrow rubric and prompting configuration, not a forecast with a deployment date.
pts.d: The supplied June 2026 working paper concerns an early-2026 experiment in Thai partnership and corporate law. Conditions include three questions, three human examiners, 15 cross-graded answers, no examiner pre-calibration, and temperature-zero, single-pass model grading without retrieval, tools, few-shot examples or chain-of-thought scaffolding. The authors acknowledge small samples, threshold-sensitive cluster counts, changing models, residual familiarity with public law and rubric materials, and incomplete determinism at temperature zero. They leave replication across jurisdictions and expert domains, as well as mitigation through fine-tuning or prompting, to future research. The authors’ broader claims of structural generality are presented alongside these scope qualifications.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct implications concern legal-NLP benchmark designers, automated assessment developers and expert grading panels; candidates are potential downstream stakeholders, not a validated deployment population.
pts.d: Benchmark researchers and developers risk treating model consensus as comprehensive coverage of expert judgement, selecting majority-aligned evaluators and interpreting legal-generation rankings through one rubric reading. Human examiners’ legitimate disagreement may be hidden by averaging or by treating one examiner as ground truth. Bar candidates and legal trainees could be affected if such systems were used for assessment, but the paper explicitly excludes individual assessment and certification uses. Its relevance to legal services is chiefly evaluation methodology and the interpretation of AI capability claims. It does not make concrete claims about law-firm staffing, legal fees, client cost savings or access to justice.
